accuracy.evidence: Every fact was computed, not typed: the lab finds factors with n % d, so 12 has pairs 1×12, 2×6, 3×4; the common factors of 24 and 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 (HCF 12); 24 and 48 are the only common multiples of 6 and 8 up to 60; 91 = 7 × 13 and 97 has no divisor among 2, 3, 5, 7. The definitions follow the Year 5 programme of study (prime, composite, factor pairs) and CCSS 4.OA.B.4, and the adult text states why primes below 10 are enough below 100 (one number in any factor pair is at most 9). Numeric items n%5, n%4, 7*k and r*c give whole answers at all corners.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented errors: odd means prime (9, 15, 21, 51 all appear), 1 is prime, omitting 1 and the number from a factor list, factors versus multiples, the product as the lowest common multiple, the HCF as any common factor, digit-based multiples (13 has a 3) and needing to test every number up to n. Each is a prediction, a lab message or a Challenge distractor.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagfpair lays n tiles into rows of a chosen width and shows a red short row whenever the width is not a factor, so factor pairs are full rectangles; it then reuses that to sort primes, adds a 1–60 grid with rings for 6s and dots for 8s, and a trial-division panel that prints n ÷ d with remainders. No other flag lab uses tile rectangles for divisibility; flagbundle groups tens and flagskip counts in 2s. The 30% shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner finds the pairs of 12 by changing the row width and seeing leftovers, then meets 7 (one row only) before the word prime is applied to it; 9 and 15 show odd composite numbers as rectangles; the common-factor step rejects 8 with the remainder for 36; the grid makes 24 visible before 48; the last step will not accept prime for 97 until 2, 3, 5 and 7 have all been tried.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 9 is prime because it is odd, the first common multiple of 6 and 8 is 48 (the product) or 14 (the sum), and testing 97 needs every number up to 96. The 3 × 3 rectangle, the 24 cell and the four-division test then disprove each, and the completion line repeats the guess.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with twelve distinct wrong-answer messages: 1 as prime (two kinds), missing 1 and 18, multiples for factors, odd 51, untested 51, product as LCM, HCF for LCM, a smaller common factor, a multiple for the HCF, a digit 7 meaning a multiple, and a factor for a multiple. Each message gives the specific check (51 ÷ 3 = 17, 17 ÷ 7 leaves 3).

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs are short and concrete (tiles, rows, rectangles) and pass the 6.5 learner limit; lab lines state one result each. Adult notes pass the validator and use the curriculum terms factor, factor pair, multiple, common factor, common multiple, prime number, composite number, highest common factor and lowest common multiple.

no_filler.evidence: Each sentence is a definition, a worked case or a check; the adult paragraphs give the standards, the method for listing pairs and testing primes, the named mistakes, and what each lab step does. The family tip is a pasta rectangle game with 24 and 23. The filler scan found nothing.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 screenshots in light and dark: the 12 tiles and the 1–60 grid fit the canvas at 390 px with readable numbers, the common-factor chips wrap to five per row on phones, the division lines fit one per row, and the row-width, prime and division buttons sit under the canvas with no clipping.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag or tap has a button twin (one fewer or one more per row, Prime and Not prime, each candidate factor, each candidate multiple, each divisor), the canvas aria-label repeats each spoken result with the remainder, and the walkthrough's axe run is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
